# Review prompt for GPT on the front-end technology stack

This file has two parts. Part 1 is for the sender: which file to attach and how to send it. Part 2 is the prompt, to be copied verbatim from the line "PROMPT START" to "PROMPT END" and pasted into the ChatGPT chat box.

This is not a review round of the business documents. The three previous rounds (`metis-review-tien-kha-thi.md`, `metis-review-vong-2.md`, `metis-review-vong-3.md`) assessed the BRD, the wireframes and the style guide. This round assesses only **one technical decision**: the front-end technology stack used to build the 58 screens of Metis into a real web application.

Goal: find counter-arguments. There is no need for GPT to confirm that the choice was right; what is needed is for GPT to point out where it will break, where it will go out of date, where it is creating its own risk, and a better alternative with evidence.

## Part 1. Sending instructions

### Send one message

1. Open a new conversation in ChatGPT. There is no need to continue the conversation of the three previous rounds: this prompt contains its own context.
2. Choose a model with a deep reasoning mode if your plan has one. **Turn on the code execution tool**, because GPT needs it to unzip the zip.
3. Paste the prompt from Part 2 into the chat box.
4. Attach `review/metis-frontend-stack-pack.zip` (21 MB, 129 files).
5. Send.

This is the only pack that needs to be sent.

### What is in the zip file

All files are in the folder `metis-frontend-stack-pack/`, keeping the exact path structure of the repo, so every relative link in the BRD and in the HTML files of the wireframes works. The pack has its own `README.md` describing the contents and the suggested reading order.

- `brd/`: the main BRD version 4.5 and the BRD addendum on onboarding version 1.1.
- `brand/`: `style-guide.md` version 0.4, `style-guide.png`, `tokens.css`, and the two logo files that the documents reference.
- `wireframes/assets/wireframe.css`: 343 lines, about 60 component classes. This is the main evidence for the Tailwind question.
- `wireframes/assets/shell.js`: 147 lines, the shared shell built from `data-*` attributes.
- `wireframes/manifest.json`, `wireframes/wireframes-digest.md`, `wireframes/README.md`.
- `wireframes/screens/`: 58 HTML files, which are exactly the markup that will be ported to React components.
- `wireframes/png/`: 58 rendered images of the screens above.

Not in the pack because they are not needed: the POC screenshots that the BRD references through `images/` (so those image links in the BRD will be broken), the three BRD review reports of the previous rounds, the `.docx` files.

### If GPT reports that it cannot view the images in the zip

In the three previous rounds GPT opened and could view the images in the zip. If it cannot this time, send the images directly into the chat box, in order of priority: `26-wbs-table`, `58-process-framework-editor`, `29-deliverable-builder`, `42-editor-states`, `31-plan-board`, `27-wbs-tree`, `11-lifecycle-framework-designer`, plus `style-guide.png`.

Official limits according to the OpenAI File Uploads FAQ (help.openai.com/en/articles/8555545): at most 512 MB per file, 20 MB per image, 80 files per 3 hours. User forums report that each message accepts at most 10 files; this figure is not yet in the official FAQ [Unverified - confirm before applying].

### Rebuilding the zip pack

The pack is made by copying the files above into a folder `metis-frontend-stack-pack/` that keeps the structure `brd/`, `brand/`, `wireframes/` and then compressing it. When the BRD, the style guide or the wireframes change, rebuild the pack before sending.

### When you receive the result

Save the Markdown file that GPT returns as `review/metis-review-frontend-stack.md`. Then work through each item in a new disposition file, in the same way as the three previous rounds did, and only then write the technical spec.

## Part 2. Prompt

---- PROMPT START ----

# Role

You are an independent technical review panel, made up of five experts working as one team:

1. **Front-end architect** for large-scale enterprise applications: has built a design system used by many teams, and has lived through at least two major front-end technology migrations.
2. **Accessibility expert** per WCAG 2.2, firmly versed in the hard ARIA patterns: `grid`, `treegrid`, drag-and-drop lists, canvases with a keyboard-equivalent path, dialogs and live regions.
3. **Performance engineer** for data-dense interfaces: tables of thousands of rows, rendering only the visible part, response time at the 95th percentile, performance on mid-range phones.
4. **Tech lead for a large team**: has managed multi-package repos for 30 people or more, and been responsible for build speed, boundary rules between packages and code quality when many people edit at the same time.
5. **Technology lifecycle assessor**: tracks which libraries are rising, standing still and dying; assesses the risk of becoming outdated within 5 years.

Task: **critique a front-end technology stack decision that the product owner has tentatively settled.** Do not praise. Every remark must be specific, backed by evidence, and come with a proposal that can be carried out. If a choice is wrong, say so directly, with the consequences and the replacement alternative. If a choice is right but for a reason different from the one the project team gave, say that too.

# Product context

**Metis** (working name) is an Enterprise Portfolio Intelligence & Governance Platform: a multi-tenant SaaS for enterprise leaders and project teams, with an MCP server (Model Context Protocol) so that customers' language assistants can work with the data through natural language.

The business documents have passed three external review rounds and are in baseline status for Discovery:

- **BRD version 4.5**: 229 requirements with IDs and acceptance criteria, of which 170 requirements belong to the first release (marked P0); 42 business rules BR-01 to BR-42; 16 roles in section 14; 51 data entities in section 15.1; 23 project metric definitions in section 12.1, 14 portfolio metrics in 12.3, 11 governance metrics in 12.4; non-functional requirements in section 17 with starting values in 17.1.
- **Supplementary BRD "Onboarding in 30 minutes" version 1.1**: 40 requirements with the prefix ONB, 27 of them in the first release; rules BR-43 to BR-53.
- **58 wireframes** at mid-fidelity level, each screen a self-contained HTML file, annotated by requirement ID, with `manifest.json` and a text digest.
- **Style guide version 0.4** with `tokens.css`: 60 design tokens, the component table in section 6, the accessibility contract in section 7a with an acceptance matrix for each interaction pattern.

Resources: an agency of about 40 developers working in parallel (assumption A-07 of the BRD). **Do not propose cutting or postponing scope because of team size.** You may still propose changing a technical choice because of risk, maintenance cost or technology lifecycle.

# Settled decisions, no critique needed

These two points are decisions of the product owner; accept them as premises:

1. **The output is a real front-end web application with sample data**, not a static prototype, and with no backend yet. It must be usable right away as a high-fidelity prototype for testing with pilot customers, and at the same time be the seed of the production front-end. The backend is settled later, in Discovery.
2. **The selection criterion is "the best", not "the least work".** The product owner said, verbatim: runs stably, few bugs, strong community, easy to maintain, explicit, easy to scale and scales fast, does not become outdated early, meets the trends of the next 5 years, runs well on every device from phone up to desktop. Every proposal of yours must be scored against exactly these nine criteria.

# The proposed technology stack, for you to critique

## Foundation layer

- React with TypeScript in strict mode (`strict`, `any` forbidden, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` enabled).
- Vite as the build tool. The application runs entirely in the browser, with no server-side rendering.
- `next` has been ruled out because the app sits behind a login, does not need to be found by search engines, and does not want to bear the cost of keeping up with the changes of the high-level router.
- Additionally packaged as an installable web app (`vite-plugin-pwa`) to be present on phones without building a native app. BRD decision D-19 excludes the native app from scope.

## Repo structure

One repo with many packages, managed with `pnpm` and `nx`:

```
packages/domain/         Pure TypeScript, no React imports: 23 metric definitions
                         of section 12.1, the permission matrix of section 14, the state machines of section 15.2,
                         the data write contract PLT-06
packages/contracts/      API contract in OpenAPI form, keyboard equivalence matrix,
                         metric definition matrix
packages/design-system/  token, component, catalog Storybook
packages/api-client/     auto-generated client, TanStack Query hooks, mock handlers
packages/fixtures/       typed sample data: tenant Acme Holdings with two workspaces
                         Creative Studio and Digital Products, tenant Nova Energy
                         for onboarding
apps/web/                one route for each screen in manifest.json
```

The reason for choosing `nx` instead of `turborepo` or `pnpm` alone: rules that block imports in the wrong direction, so that the rule "the domain package must not import the UI package" becomes a build error rather than a verbal agreement in a team of 40 people.

## User interface

- **Tailwind CSS** for the whole app. This is a decision of the product owner, chosen in place of the CSS Modules option.
- `brand/tokens.css` is kept unchanged as the single source of color, typography, density and focus ring; Tailwind reads these CSS variables.
- The set `wireframes/assets/wireframe.css` (30 KB, 343 lines, about 60 component classes such as `.kpi`, `.chip`, `.table`, `.board`, `.canvas`, `.pipeline`, `.fresh`, `.save`, `.src`) will be translated into React components using Tailwind. This CSS set has passed three external review rounds and currently corresponds one to one with the component table in section 6 of the style guide.
- `storybook` as the living catalog of the design system, running together with interaction tests and the accessibility checker.
- Icon set: not chosen yet. Style guide section 9 says "wireframes use text symbols; choose an icon set with a 1,5px stroke when building the app".
- Dark mode: not designed yet (style guide section 9).

## Interactive components

- **React Aria Components** for dialogs, side drawers, menus, select, combobox, date picker, tooltip, toasts.
- **A self-built dense table**, no commercial library bought. The base is TanStack Table for the model (columns, branch expansion, filtering, sorting, row selection) plus TanStack Virtual to render only the visible rows, plus a self-written layer of keyboard handling and screen reader labels following the acceptance matrix in section 7a of the style guide. It applies to three screens: the work breakdown tree table, the project portfolio table, the change request register. **The option of buying AG Grid Enterprise was ruled out** because there is no wish to depend on a vendor and no wish to pay per developer.
- `@xyflow/react` as the drawing layer for the four canvases, plus `elkjs` to lay out diagrams automatically. The graph is a TypeScript model in the domain package; the canvas is one way to view it, the list editor is the second way to view it.
- A self-built drag-and-drop board on top of React Aria.
- `react-hook-form` with `zod` for the long forms (a charter with 9 sections, a work item form with more than 20 fields, the change request form).

## Data

- One API contract file in the OpenAPI standard in `packages/contracts/` as the single source, generating four things automatically: TypeScript types, a runtime data validator using `zod`, API call hooks, and mock handlers for Mock Service Worker.
- TanStack Query for all data fetched from the server; `zustand` for a few small UI state stores.
- `tRPC` has been ruled out because it forces the backend to be TypeScript, while the BRD has not settled the backend.
- `xstate` for six state machines: the change request lifecycle, the tenant lifecycle, the workspace lifecycle, the process framework lifecycle, the save-and-conflict machine of PLT-05 and PLT-06, the five-step flow of onboarding. Reason: section 15.2 of the BRD already lists the lists of states and the transition rules.

## Language, dates

- `i18next` with `react-i18next` and formatting in the ICU standard. English by default, Vietnamese second, strings separated from the code from the first commit.
- `date-fns` for dates and time zones. Switch to the browser's `Temporal` API when it becomes widespread.

## Testing and automated gates

- `vitest` for the domain package, including the metric cross-check test (at the same point in time, the metrics on the Overview, Focus, Board screens and the report must be equal) and permission tests generated from the role matrix.
- `playwright` for real interaction on three browser engines and on a phone viewport.
- `axe-core` in Playwright and in Storybook.
- Image comparison of each screen against the 58 images in `wireframes/png/`.
- Tests generated from data: each row of the keyboard equivalence matrix generates one test.
- Requirement coverage gate: a script reads `manifest.json` and breaks the build if a screen has no route yet or a first-release requirement has no screen yet.
- `eslint` with `prettier`; `biome` has been ruled out because it is less mature.

## Deliberately ruled out

Material UI and component sets that have their own visual language; CSS-in-JS libraries that run at runtime (`styled-components`, `emotion`); `create-react-app`; `moment`; `enzyme`.

# Technical constraints that the technology stack must meet

This is the most important part for you to score feasibility. Every item is quoted from BRD version 4.5 or style guide version 0.4.

## Work breakdown tree table, screen `26-wbs-table`

BRD section 18.3 itself rates this screen "High" in difficulty, and rates the canvas "Very high". Requirements WBS-04, WBS-05, WBS-06, WBS-18, WBS-19, WBS-20 together demand:

- A table in tree form, at most 5 levels; the Category node exists only at level 1 and is excluded from every count.
- Inline editing of every column except code and duration, with a date picker in the cell.
- The code column and the name column stay fixed when scrolling horizontally.
- Filtering by Category, Phase, Type, Status, PIC, applied immediately without an Apply button, and a matching row still keeps its parent rows.
- Select many rows and then change Status, PIC, Phase, Priority, Risk Level in bulk; deletion with a confirmation that lists the children and links that will be lost.
- Views that can be saved (filters, columns, sorting, branch expansion state), a personal type and a type shared with the whole project; plus three column presets.
- Two density levels: 36px rows in comfortable mode, 32px in compact mode, saved per person.
- Fully operable by keyboard, following the model in section 7a of the style guide: arrow keys move between cells, `Enter` or the quick-edit key enters edit mode, `Esc` cancels, `Space` selects the row, the left and right arrows open and close branches; the column header is read when the cell changes.
- A cell locked by the baseline shows a lock icon; editing it opens the change request flow rather than editing in place.
- Performance per section 17.1: usable within 2 seconds at the 95th percentile with a project of up to 2000 work items.
- The acceptance matrix in section 7a demands that it state clearly: the roles and relations of cells, rows, headers; the branch expansion state and the level of each row; the reading order when there are fixed columns; sorting and filtering announced through the live region with the number of remaining rows; the cell being edited and how to cancel.

## Four canvases, the screens `27-wbs-tree`, `29-deliverable-builder`, `11-lifecycle-framework-designer`, `58-process-framework-editor`

- Rule BR-41 and requirement BLD-13 demand an **equivalence matrix**: each canvas operation is a row, including the mouse gesture, the keyboard command, the action in the list editor, and the command sent to the server. The list of operations is already listed in BLD-13: create, edit, move nodes between lanes, reorder nodes, set or remove a parent node, add, rename, reorder, delete lanes, create a link and set its type and lag, delete a link, add, move, delete routing points.
- The acceptance criterion of BLD-13 says, verbatim: every row of the matrix must be runnable in the list editor by keyboard alone, and no editor operation may exist that the matrix does not list.
- Requirement WBS-08 demands two kinds of automatic diagram layout, vertical and horizontal, plus zoom and full-screen mode. WBS-09 demands a free node-dragging mode and positions remembered across sessions.
- Requirement BLD-03 demands a single start date that drives the dates of every node, according to the day offset of each node.

## Save state, conflicts, permissions, screens `42-editor-states` and `43-access-states`

- PLT-05: every editable screen shows the save state in the same place, including saving, saved with the time, save failed with the reason and a retry button; leaving the page while unsaved changes remain asks for confirmation.
- PLT-06: a single data write contract for the app, for MCP and for the API. Each write command carries the version number of the record it is based on, plus an idempotency key. An old version is rejected together with the newer value. A conflict appears right at the field, not as a toast, with three choices: keep mine, take the other person's, merge.
- PLT-04: the three permission states must carry a reason and a next action, and must not show an empty page: no access with a request-access button, read-only with a specific reason, session expired with a sign-in-again box without losing the data being typed.

## Metrics and data freshness

- Rule BR-32: every metric shown in the product or returned through MCP follows the definitions in section 12 and can be traced back to the source record.
- Rule BR-39: every dashboard, report, PDF file and answer of the language assistant states the data timestamp and the version of the metric definition; a saved version is a snapshot and does not change when the data changes.
- The acceptance criterion of OVW-01 says the values of the metric tiles must equal the health summary part of the weekly report for the same day.
- Style guide section 6 defines four data freshness levels, each with a shape, text and color, never by color alone.

## Phone up to desktop

Style guide section 5.1 settles three width levels: from 1280px the full layout; 768 to 1279px the sidebar collapses to an icon column, tables keep the code and name columns fixed, the other columns scroll horizontally; under 768px one column, tables turn into cards, touch targets at least 44 by 44px, and only the reading screens plus light updates per D-19: Focus, Board as a list, Overview, My approvals.

## Accessibility

The proposed target is WCAG 2.2 level AA, settled in decision D-26. Section 7a of the style guide has a contract for six patterns: editable table, navigation tree, board, canvas, dialog and drawer, live region. Each pattern must also have its own acceptance matrix, each row a testable behavior, with an automated test and a pass with a real screen reader before the pilot. Placeholder text in input fields counts as meaningful text, so it must meet the contrast threshold.

## Scale of the screen set

58 screens, divided into six areas: access and tenant (13 screens), workspace and governance (8 screens), portfolio (10 screens), project execution (15 screens), personal and collaboration (3 screens), onboarding (9 screens). Among them are screens of phases V2 and V3, currently labeled "Planned" rather than being disabled buttons.

# The nine points the project team itself admits are weak, for you to examine first

Speaking plainly and without defending anything: these are nine places where the project team itself feels unsure. Assess each one, and add the ones the team has not seen.

1. **Image comparison against the 58 mid-fidelity wireframes.** A high-fidelity application will never match a mid-fidelity wireframe pixel by pixel, so this image comparison gate may be useless or noisy. A different comparison mechanism is needed: structural comparison, or comparison of the component list, or the app's own baseline images.
2. **Tailwind erases the one-to-one link with the style guide.** Section 6 of the style guide is currently a component table that the client has examined over three rounds, and `wireframe.css` currently has exactly one file for each row of that table. When moving to utility classes, this link is lost, unless a new traceability mechanism is defined. What is that mechanism?
3. **The self-built tree table is now the biggest risk of the project.** After the commercial library was ruled out, the hardest part is in the team's hands. Assess honestly: can TanStack Table plus TanStack Virtual plus a self-written ARIA layer achieve the whole list of requirements above, how long will it take, and what are the specific traps (fixed columns with virtualized rows, the screen reader reading order when there are fixed columns, inline editing in a `treegrid`, filtering that still keeps parent rows, two density levels)?
4. **`xstate` may be overkill.** Do six state machines justify the learning cost and the maintenance cost, or are plain transition functions plus data types enough?
5. **The API contract is written before the backend exists.** The front-end will invent the API by itself, and then the backend team in Discovery may do it differently. Is this risk worth bearing, or should it be done another way?
6. **The keyboard equivalence matrix does not exist yet.** BRD section 18.4 makes it a product of Discovery. So tests generated from the matrix cannot be generated yet. Should the matrix be made first, or the editor built first and the matrix extracted from it?
7. **Dark mode is not designed yet and the icon set is not chosen yet.** These two affect how tokens and components are organized. Should they be settled before writing the first component, or left for later?
8. **Sample data must be consistent across the 58 screens.** The wireframes are currently consistent by hand. In the app, the sample data lives in a separate package, but who keeps it matching the wireframes, and matching the figures printed in the BRD (for example 16 items and 15 links of the CGI Still Renders framework, 34 projects and 214,6 million EUR of Nova Energy)?
9. **There is no decision yet on the front-end operations infrastructure**: where to store the login token, content security policy, bundle splitting, bundle size budget, feature flags, error collection and real-user measurements, React error boundaries, PDF export on the client side or the server side (BRD decision D-13 chose the server side), file upload and malware scanning.

# Tasks

## S1. Score the technology stack against the product owner's nine criteria

One table, each row a layer of the technology stack (foundation, repo, UI, interactive components, data, language, testing). Each row is scored 1 to 5 for each criterion: stable, few bugs, community, easy to maintain, explicit, easy to scale, scales fast, 5-year lifecycle, phone up to desktop. Include one sentence of reasoning for each score below 4.

## S2. Critique of the framework choice

Is React really the best choice for **this product**, or only the safest choice? Consider Vue 3, Svelte 5, Angular and SolidJS as well. The argument must rest on the three hard widgets (tree table, canvas, board) and on the team size of 40 people, not on sentiment. If you change the choice, state clearly what must additionally be written compared with React.

## S3. Critique of the Tailwind decision

This section needs a large amount of space.

- Is translating 343 lines of CSS that have passed three review rounds into utility classes worth it, and what does it lose or keep?
- Which traceability mechanism preserves the link between the component table in section 6 of the style guide and the code after using Tailwind? State a concrete option.
- How should Tailwind read tokens from `tokens.css` correctly, and which tokens cannot be mapped to Tailwind (for example `--focus-ring` is a two-layer shadow, or the set of 7 status color groups with 3 values each)?
- The markup of the dense table and of the canvas when written with utility classes: is it readable, is it maintainable with 40 people?
- What Tailwind does not solve in this project, so that the product owner knows what they are buying.
- If you believe the project should go back to CSS Modules or use a third option (for example plain CSS with cascade layers, or a library that generates classes at build time), say so clearly and give the migration path.

## S4. Critique of the decision to self-build the dense table

- List each requirement of the tree table in the constraints part and say to what degree TanStack Table plus TanStack Virtual meets it: available out of the box, must be written by hand, or not feasible.
- State the specific technical traps, especially ARIA for a `treegrid` combined with virtualized rows and fixed columns.
- Estimate the effort as a range, state the assumptions clearly, attach the label "estimate".
- Compare honestly with three other options: AG Grid Enterprise, Glide Data Grid, and a fully self-built table without TanStack. State clearly which of the nine criteria each option wins on.
- Say whether the decision to rule out the commercial library should be revisited, and if so under what conditions.

## S5. Critique of the canvas plan

- Can `@xyflow/react` plus `elkjs` meet the four canvases with their four different sets of requirements, or do these four screens need two different approaches?
- Is the model "the graph is our model, the canvas and the list are two ways to view it" really the only way to satisfy the equivalence matrix? State another way if there is one.
- How far does the keyboard support of `@xyflow/react` go today; what must be written by hand? Attach [Needs verification] if you are not sure about the current version.
- The situation where two people edit one canvas at the same time: BRD section 20 states the solution as "one person edits a canvas at a time". Assess this solution.

## S6. Critique of the data and contract plan

- Is the chain "one OpenAPI file generates four things" robust? Name the specific tool for each generation step and say which tools are well maintained at the moment.
- The front-end inventing the contract by itself before the backend exists: what is the real risk, and how can it be reduced?
- Is Mock Service Worker suitable for both the test environment and the demo environment for customers, or is a separate mock server needed?
- Are TanStack Query plus `zustand` enough; where will they fall short?
- Assess `xstate` for the six state machines: keep, reduce to how many machines, or drop.

## S7. Critique of the repo structure and build tools

- `nx` versus `turborepo` versus `pnpm` alone: which one wins on the criteria of ease of maintenance and explicitness with 40 people, and why?
- Do the five proposed packages have the right boundaries? Point out which package will bloat, which should be split, which does not need to exist.
- Build speed and test run speed when the repo is large: where will it become slow first?
- How to divide the work among 40 people on this structure: who edits which package, and which rules prevent conflicts?

## S8. Critique of the testing strategy

- Does the proposed testing pyramid have the right proportions; what is missing, what is superfluous?
